title: How induction works
objective: Use a base case and a clear k-to-k+1 step to prove the result.

blocks.text: Idea in plain language

Induction proves a statement for every positive integer. First prove P(1). Next assume P(k) for an arbitrary positive integer k; this is the induction hypothesis. Use that assumption to prove P(k+1). Since the base is true and each true case leads to the next, every positive-integer case follows.
Worked proof

blocks.title: One step at a time
blocks.problem: Explain why checking P(1), P(2), and P(3) alone is not a proof for all positive integers.

steps.explanation: These checks establish only three cases. They do not address P(4) or any later integer.
The induction step must work for an arbitrary positive integer k, rather than just one tested value.
Together, the base case and the general step let the argument reach 2, 3, 4, and every later positive integer.

blocks.answer: A few examples are evidence; a base case plus a valid general step is a proof.

blocks.question: What must be proved first in induction starting at n=1?
blocks.explanation: The first required case is the base case P(1). Without it, the implication P(k) ⇒ P(k+1) has no starting point from which to propagate.

blocks.question: What may you assume in the induction step?
options: P(k) is true for an arbitrary k
blocks.explanation: State the induction hypothesis P(k) for an arbitrary positive integer k. Then use that assumption to derive P(k+1), rather than assuming the conclusion you are trying to prove.

title: Sum of the first n integers
objective: Use a base case and a clear k-to-k+1 step to prove the result.

blocks.text: Idea in plain language

The formula 1+2+⋯+n=n(n+1)/2 counts consecutive integers. For induction, the next sum is the old sum plus k+1. Substitute the hypothesis for the old sum, take a common denominator, and factor until it matches the formula with n replaced by k+1.
Worked proof

blocks.title: One step at a time

steps.explanation: At n=1, both sides equal 1, so the base case holds.
Assume this formula for an arbitrary k≥1.
The next sum is the previous sum plus its new last term.
Use a common denominator and factor out k+1; this is the required formula at n=k+1.

blocks.answer: The base and the step both hold, so the formula is true for all n≥1.

check.explanation: This final expression is the exact target at k+1; the base case starts the chain.

blocks.text: Review this lesson
Try both questions after explaining the base case and induction step aloud. Check which term is added when k changes to k+1 and why the final expression matches the target.

blocks.question: What term is added when the sum ends at k+1 instead of k?
blocks.explanation: The sum through k+1 contains every old term 1 through k and one new last term, k+1. Thus S(k+1)=S(k)+(k+1).

blocks.question: If S(k)=k(k+1)/2, what is S(k+1)?
blocks.explanation: Add k+1 to the assumed sum: k(k+1)/2 + (k+1) = [k(k+1)+2(k+1)]/2. Factor k+1 to obtain (k+1)(k+2)/2, exactly the formula with n=k+1.

blocks.title: Proof in one line
blocks.text: The base and the step both hold, so the formula is true for all n≥1.

title: Squares and odd-number sums
objective: Use a base case and a clear k-to-k+1 step to prove the result.

blocks.text: Idea in plain language

Two common induction identities are 1²+2²+⋯+n²=n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 and 1+3+⋯+(2n−1)=n². For either proof, check n=1, assume the formula at k, add the next term, then simplify to the expression at k+1. The next square is (k+1)²; the next odd number is 2k+1.
Worked proof

blocks.title: One step at a time

steps.explanation: The base case n=1 is true.
Assume the identity for an arbitrary positive integer k.
The next odd number after 2k−1 is 2k+1; replace the old sum using the hypothesis.
Factor the perfect square. This is the claimed formula at n=k+1.

blocks.answer: The identity holds for every positive integer n.

check.explanation: This final expression is the exact target at k+1; the base case starts the chain.

blocks.text: Review this lesson
Try both questions after explaining the base case and induction step aloud. Check which term is added when k changes to k+1 and why the final expression matches the target.

blocks.question: What is the next odd term after 2k−1?
blocks.explanation: Consecutive odd numbers differ by 2. Adding 2 to 2k−1 gives 2k+1; this is the term needed to pass from k odd terms to k+1 odd terms.

blocks.question: What must the square-sum proof reach at n=k+1?
blocks.explanation: Start with n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 and substitute n=k+1 everywhere. The target becomes (k+1)(k+2)(2k+3)/6. The induction algebra must simplify to this expression.

blocks.title: Proof in one line
blocks.text: The identity holds for every positive integer n.

title: Geometric sums by induction
objective: Use a base case and a clear k-to-k+1 step to prove the result.

blocks.text: Idea in plain language

For 1+5+5²+⋯+5^(n−1), there are n terms and the last is 5^(n−1). The proposed sum is (5^n−1)/4. In the induction step add the next term 5^k, write it with denominator 4, then combine the powers. The formula is valid because 5 is the common ratio.
Worked proof

blocks.title: One step at a time

steps.explanation: At n=1 the left side has one term, 1; the right side is also 1.
Assume the formula for an arbitrary k≥1.
The new sum includes one more term, 5^k.
Combine five copies of 5^k into 5^(k+1), matching the target at n=k+1.

blocks.answer: The geometric-sum formula holds for every n≥1.

check.explanation: This final expression is the exact target at k+1; the base case starts the chain.

blocks.text: Review this lesson
Try both questions after explaining the base case and induction step aloud. Check which term is added when k changes to k+1 and why the final expression matches the target.

blocks.question: What is the added term when the sum grows from n=k to n=k+1?
blocks.explanation: At n=k, the final term is 5^(k−1). One more term in the sequence multiplies by 5, giving 5^k. Add that to the induction hypothesis.

blocks.question: Simplify (5^k−1)/4 + 5^k.
blocks.explanation: Put both terms over 4: (5^k−1+4·5^k)/4 = (5·5^k−1)/4. Since 5·5^k=5^(k+1), the result is (5^(k+1)−1)/4.

blocks.title: Proof in one line
blocks.text: The geometric-sum formula holds for every n≥1.
Remember

For 1+5+5²+⋯+5^(n−1), there are n terms and the last is 5^(n−1). The proposed sum is (5^n−1)/4. In the induction step add the next term 5^k, write it with denominator 4, then combine the powers. The formula is valid because 5 is the common ratio.

flashcards.back: At n=k, the final term is 5^(k−1). One more term in the sequence multiplies by 5, giving 5^k. Add that to the induction hypothesis.
